The test image shows two tomato stems cut/split longitudinally at the base, revealing:
- Brown/tan discoloration of the internal vascular/pith tissue
- Darkened crown/stem junction area
- Fibrous root system with brown roots
- No visible white mycelium or fluffy growth

This pattern of internal vascular browning in split stems is characteristic of a vascular wilt disease. Most likely candidates: Verticillium Wilt, Bacterial Wilt, or Southern Bacterial Wilt.

Using my 1 reference image on Verticillium Wilt to confirm:

The Verticillium Wilt reference shows above-ground foliar yellowing/chlorosis symptoms, which is different from the test image presentation. However, Verticillium Wilt is classically diagnosed by cutting the stem and observing the brown vascular discoloration — exactly what the test image shows.

**Analysis:**
- Test image: two stems split longitudinally at the base, revealing brown/tan internal vascular tissue discoloration, with brownish roots
- No white mycelium (rules out Southern Blight, Sclerotinia)
- No leaf spots/blotches visible (not Septoria, Early Blight, etc.)
- Showing stem cross-section vascular browning — hallmark diagnostic presentation of Verticillium Wilt
- The crown/stem base discoloration with fibrous roots matches Verticillium crown rot symptoms

The stem cross-section showing brown xylem streaking at the plant base is the classic diagnostic method for Verticillium Wilt.
